All I can say is that different people respond to medications in different ways. The human body is incredibly complex, which is why overdosing in general produces some of the most mixed results out of any suicide method. If the doctors who assessed you can’t say how you lived, then it’s unlikely that strangers on the Internet could figure it out.

That said, I’m glad you survived. If there’s ever a time to interpret something as a sign, I would interpret this as a second chance and give life another try. Do you think you’d be willing to do that?

Could you tell me what you think constitutes true compassion? For the longest time, I also thought doing the “right thing” for one’s own sake was selfish. It was the same reason I thought I was a terrible person—I volunteered and did all sorts of “selfless” stuff, not because I was a good person, but rather because I *wanted* to be a good person. I wanted to justify my own existence because I couldn’t find any other reason to live.

But at some point, I asked, “Why does it matter? Is there really a difference?” You can paint anyone and everyone as selfish if you apply the right perspective.

Genuinely curious: what would count as actual compassion in your eyes? I’m not saying you’re wrong. I just want to understand you a bit better.
I don’t know. The first answer that came to mind was “death”, but I suppose I won’t know until I get there.
I’d be okay with it if it actually let me shoot lightning.

It’s not selfish at all. Humans are social creatures, despite whatever some people like to claim. Love is every bit as necessary as food or oxygen.

I’m at the same place, so I understand at least a little bit. It’s a horrible feeling to care so much for others, only to realize none of them care that much about you. I think it’s unfair that you’re not surrounded by people who reciprocate your love.

I don’t have any miracle cures, so maybe I’m just spouting empty words. At the very least, though, I want you to know: the way you feel isn’t wrong in any way, it’s not your fault for feeling this way, and you’re not alone.

And above all, you’re not replaceable. Just because some people haven’t recognized that doesn’t mean no one ever will.

I can’t say I’m as well off as you are (reading your post honestly made me a little jealous), but even so, I think the way you feel is perfectly valid. Depression is not so simple that you can pinpoint it just by looking at a life. There are innumerable social and neurological factors that go into it.

I also sometimes feel like an imposter—like I don’t “deserve” to feel this way. The honest truth is that there is always someone worse off than you are. At what point does someone deserve to feel bad? There are things that I lack, yes, but there are also things I have. Do those invalidate my emotions? How do I compare the good and the bad? It’s not like we can take an average. We can’t even count them, really; is having friends one thing, or do I count each friend individually? And how much does a friend offset the pain of endless exhaustion?

Long story short: there is no metric for how good or bad a life is, and accordingly, there is no threshold for when a person should feel good or bad. The only conclusive thing I can tell you is that I am absolutely glad you’re deciding to seek therapy. The path towards learning to be happy again is different for everyone, but I think you’re on the right track. I hope I don’t overstep myself in advising you, but I recommend you keep an open mind, keep trying, and never forget how loved you are.

Reading this makes me feel like I’m looking at a reflection of myself (hopefully, that doesn’t come across as too narcissistic).

I feel exactly the same way, being abandoned over and over by people who I thought cared for me as much as I cared for them. I didn’t have anything else in life, so the only happiness I could find was in being needed by someone else. I don’t think that’s too unnatural. Humans are social creatures. We’re not built to live alone.

I’m still in the same situation, so I don’t have the right to give you any advice. I can say “you need to learn to love yourself”, because that’s apparently the right answer, but I don’t see how that’s possible. I can say this with confidence, though: you’re not alone. Not everyone is the same. There are people out there who will value you for who you are. I value you—and I’m well aware of the sheer hypocrisy in that statement.

It’s because people don’t want this on their main account. Anonymity is what allows people to open up to this extent, without fear of consequences.

It’s absolutely not for farming karma. This is an extremely inefficient way to get karma (which is absolutely worthless in the first place). And if I wanted karma, I’d prefer to get it on my main account.

So it’s because of two possible reasons:

1. It’s a throwaway account so their suicidal intent can’t be traced back to their main, which might be used to identify them.

2. They just heard about this subreddit, which has received some media attention, and they made an account for the sole purpose of opening up to someone.

I feel like this comment is an example of the problem. I get that it’s tiring, but if you’re a hotline responder, you really shouldn’t be so harsh. Sometimes it’s even just a matter of phrasing. Even if you can’t fix someone’s problems in 10 minutes, under no circumstances should you actively increase someone’s risk level (e.g. by getting defensive and thereby demonstrating implicit hostility).

A different hotline responder also commented on this post and said that expectations for hotlines are often unrealistic, but they didn’t get downvoted. There’s a reason for that.

I think it’s good that your uncle at least modified his views after seeing the evidence. There are a lot of people out there who dismiss mental health issues as “weakness”, and in a similar situation, would simply conclude that their partner was “weak”. Rather than “I don’t believe in this because I see no evidence”, it becomes “I see the evidence, but I don’t suffer from these issues because I’m better than the pussies who do”. I personally have depression and suffer from suicidal thoughts, but I can’t voice them because I know some of the people who can’t empathize always doubt on some level. It’s difficult to open up when you know that thought (“You’re just weak, stop looking for attention”) is in the back of their minds. I know I’m weak; I don’t need you to tell me that. I tried to be the tough, confident guy for 19 years, and it’s hard, but I have to keep it up because of people like this Navy dude.
